ResponsesInList.Title: Another bug de-bugged (JCLOZE/JMATCH)
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi folks, I found another bug that was causing the Cloze function not to work properly, but first some background info... The hotpot module works by scanning the code of the .htm file that you have created with Hot Potatoes and adding special code to it. It does this in two steps, 1) the scan attempts to detect which Hot Pot module the file is for. This isn't so easy because the code itself for many modules nowhere explicitly says "This is the JMATCH module" etc. so I've got to find a snippet of code that appears to be unique to that module in order to identify it. 2) After it has determined what module it is working with, then it continues to look further down in the code to find the appropriate place to insert the code for outputting the results. This, too, varies from module to module. Now, it turns out that the snippet of code that I was using to search for the JMatch module also existed in the JCLOZE module. Thus the .HTM file was wrongly identified and the code never found the appropriate place to insert the Moodle output code. The file that is attached here goes inside moodle/mod/hotpot. Could some of you who were having problems try this and report back? It works for me, but hey, with computers that often doesn't mean much!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Suggestions??
ResponsesInList.Text: I've just posted a revision which includes a new 'mod.html' file although the error that you cite is new to me. Please try the new file and see if it cures the problem. I'm sorry to say that I still haven't included backup capability with the hotpot module, but I am working on it. I should have a working version before the end of September, although this won't help Jim. If you are familiar with the mysql database, however, you might be able to transfer all of the files from one database or course to another, particularly if you are not interested in keeping the associated user records. You can transfer the entire mdl_hotpot table to your new database manually. Once this has been done, then you will need to modify the course number for each entry *if* the course number has changed. You can do this semi-automatically. For example, in the old database, if the course id was 3 and now it should be 4, you do this: update mdl_hotpot set course = 4 where course = 3 There is another table mdl_course_modules that has a single line entry for each hotpot instance. You might be able to extract these from your old table and add them to the new one. The 'course' field has to be modified as above. In additon, the 'instance' field has to contain the 'id' number of the activity from the mdl_hotpot table. There is a slight chance that the module number for 'hotpot' might have also changed. You can see what the current module number for hotpot activities is by checking the 'id' in the mdl_modules table. Even with all of this fiddling, however, you will still have to modify the start and end dates manually for each activity, unless old times are still applicable to your new school term. I hope this helps.

ResponsesInList.Text: Don The biggest differences is that with hotpot there is very little in the way of student tracking/control. Hotpot tests are for fun, unless one joins the online tracking service that they provide at a fee, or oen uses Thomas Robbs great extension module to allow Hotpot quizzes to be added to Moodle. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Learn Moodle or Hot Potatoes First?
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the background, Tim. I wonder that for raw beginners that eventually I want to use Moodle, should I go for short term "fun" with HOTPOT or long term happiness with Moodle? Is HOTPOT easier for them to set up (ie. no server )?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Learn Moodle or Hot Potatoes First?
ResponsesInList.Text: short term "fun" with HOTPOT or long term happiness with Moodle Yes, I think this is exactly the trade-off that you're facing. HotPots allow beginners to have stunning results at a cost of a very short learning curve (especially if you do not introduce things like the CGI reporting, the advanced mode of JQuiz or the hybrid questions). Once they get a good grasp of the basics, they may venture into more difficult Hotpot customization. On the other hand, Moodle requires a little more training time, but in the long run can be much more rewarding (because it is not just a quizzing tool, but a full-blown CMS) So, I think it very much depends on who your trainees are and how much they are motivated to use ICT to enhance their teaching. If they are resistant, show them the basics of Hotpots first, get them hooked and then tell them about Moodle. If they are determined to learn how to use ICT in teaching, you may as well start with Moodle. Hope this helps, Przemek

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Learn Moodle or Hot Potatoes First?
ResponsesInList.Text: You'd normally want to put your hotpot quizzes on a server anyway, although it would be possible to put them directly on the students' machines or in a common file area. This, of course, would be a violation of the Hot Potatoes license, which states that you have to make your material publicly available if you want to use if for free. This, of course, means putting the stuff on a publicly accessibel server. Of course, a LOT more people have access to web servers than they do Moodle servers but teaching them how to create Hot Pot activities must go hand in hand with teaching them how to create a website and how to upload their files to it. If Moodle is available, then there is no need to learn how to FTP files, or to create a home page from which the Hotpot files can be accessed.

Thanks to the "Moodle for Language Teachers" participants. it has been now tested on a wide variety of browsers, so should work. Thanks go to Peter Ruthven-Stuart, Jean-Pierre Pawlak, Peter Sereinigg for their help in testing it, and to Timothy Takemoto for his enthusiastic encouragement of the project. Please report any problems that you have with it to me, and I will try to deal with them as soon as I can. What follows is the contents of the READ.ME file. Unfortunately, I had trouble uploading the file as an attachment, so please take it from: http://tomrobb.com/HotPot.zip ------------------------------------------ This is version 1.1 (2004/02/20) of a new Hot Potatoes module. It should work with Moodle versions 1.1.1 and 1.2dev although perhaps not with any releases since mid-January 2004.

ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Tom, I have a question about Hotpot quizes.  Where does the answer checking take place?  Is it on the server ?  Or does the Javascript downloaded onto the client computer do the checking?  If the latter, then it would be possible to cheat by tampering with the downloaded Javascript. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: New Module: Hotpot
ResponsesInList.Text: Zig asks, e does the answer checking take place?  Is it on the server?  Or does the Javascript downloaded onto the client computer do the checking?  If the latter, then it would be possible to cheat by tampering with the downloaded Javascript. Checking is done via javascript on the client side, and no, the students couldn't cheat by tampering with the code because it will only record the scores in Moodle it is is properly set in a Moodle framed document that invokes a Moodle script that requires them to be logged on, etc. Now with one of the modules, JCROSS which makes crossword puzzles, one can see the correct answers through 'View Source' but for the other modules, there is a simple, but most likely, effective, encoding scheme to prevent cheating. I should point out, though, that Hot Potatoes was originally conceived as a program for PRACTICE and REVIEW rather than for testing. Still, however, if the instructor is assigning these activities for practice, s/he needs a way of knowing whether the students have done the work and how successful they were in doing it. Thus the Moodle tracking feature is still important.

ResponsesInList.Text: Just to play devil's advocate: I agree that Javascript tampering would be beyond the capabilities of the vast majority of students. However in principle it would be possible to write a browser plugin which would do the tampering on the fly. Perhaps there might be an economic incentive for somebody to write such a plugin. Of course if Hotpot is used for practice and review there is no problem. But if it is used for assessment, I think one ought to be mindful of such a potential limitation.

ResponsesInList.Title: HotPot version 1.4beta now available
ResponsesInList.Text: This version addresses most of Martin's requests for improvements. Availability dates have now been implemented in the same fashion as other modules. File selection is via a pop-up dialog box. The "View Results" page now allows the instructor to delete specific records via checkboxes, or to delete all records via a "Delete all" button. HotPot now supports TexToys (WebSequitur and WebRhubarb) Note that the lang/en/hotpot.php file must be updated in order for this feature to display properly The language file is now smaller, with most definitions being read from the 'quiz.php' file when they already exist there. A bug in some XP installations which resulted the tail end of the target HTM file not being read in has been 'fixed' by forcing multiple rows of spaces to be written at the end of the file. (an awkward kludge at best, but it works!) Please see the included README file for information on how to newly install or update your current version. The module has also been committed to CVS . ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Importing for HotPot
ResponsesInList.Text: The way the HotPot module is built is that it imports the HTML files that you create with HotPot version 6, so the look & feel of the original pages is still there. HotPot files with embedded media should work as long as the resources are still in the same relative location to the HotPot file. When you import a HotPot HTML file, it is stored in your course file area. Then when you create the HotPot activity in your course using the "ADD"/"HotPot" selection, a modified version of your original HotPot file is created inside a "hotpot" directory inside the course directory. (The original file stays where it was, untouched.) The sound and video resources would have to be placed in the same relative location to this modified version of your original HTML file. Thus, if the resources were orginally in the same directory as your hotpot file, then they will need to be uploaded ot the 'hotpot' directory inside your course file area. Let me know if this isn't sufficiently clear. As for Vinny's question, no Quandry2 mazes aren't currently handled.
